interactions.label: The remarkably tight fit between the maternal pelvis and the fetal head in human

params.question: The remarkably tight fit between the maternal pelvis and the fetal head in humans is primarily the result of which evolutionary compromise?

answers.text: Reduced ligament flexibility in the human pelvis compared to quadrupedal mammals

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. While ligament properties differ across species, the primary constraint is skeletal — the bony pelvis was narrowed for bipedal gait while the fetal skull enlarged for brain development.

answers.text: Decreased pelvic depth as an adaptation to erect posture

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. The critical compromise is between pelvic width (narrowed for bipedal locomotion) and fetal skull size (enlarged for neocortical development), not pelvic depth alone.

answers.text: Narrowed pelvis for upright bipedal gait combined with an enlarged fetal skull for brain development

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Upright bipedal locomotion narrowed the bony pelvis, while expansion of the neocortex enlarged the fetal skull — creating a tight fit that demands specific cardinal movements for successful delivery.

answers.text: Decreased fetal brain size to facilitate passage through the birth canal

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Fetal brain size actually increased during human evolution (neocortex expansion), which is precisely one half of the compromise that creates the tight fit.

overallFeedback.feedback: The tight fit exists because evolution narrowed the pelvis for upright walking while simultaneously enlarging the fetal skull for brain development. This is the central mechanical problem of human childbirth and the reason the cardinal movements evolved.

Exactly right. This evolutionary compromise — narrower pelvis for bipedal gait, larger skull for brain development — is why human labour requires the cardinal movements (specific rotations and flexions) to navigate the birth canal.

params.question: Labour that begins spontaneously at 38 weeks with a cephalic presentation but requires vacuum-assisted delivery is classified as normal labour.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This is false. Normal labour requires completion without ANY operative intervention. Vacuum-assisted delivery is an instrumental (operative) procedure. All four criteria — spontaneous onset, cephalic presentation, term gestation, and no operative intervention — must be met simultaneously for labour to qualify as 'normal'.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct — this is false. Normal labour must satisfy ALL four criteria: spontaneous onset, cephalic presentation, term gestation, AND completion without operative intervention. Vacuum extraction is an instrumental delivery, so despite meeting the other three criteria, this labour falls outside the definition of 'normal'.

interactions.label: A labouring woman's WHO partograph shows satisfactory cervical dilatation on the

params.question: A labouring woman's WHO partograph shows satisfactory cervical dilatation on the cervicograph, but the fetal heart rate drops to 100 beats per minute. Which section of the partograph first alerts you to this abnormality?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The fetal condition section records fetal heart rate (every 30 minutes in the first stage, every 5 minutes in the second stage), liquor colour, and degree of moulding. A drop to 100 bpm is detected here, independent of the satisfactory progress shown on the cervicograph.

Incorrect. The progress of labour section tracks cervical dilatation (cervicograph), descent by station, and contraction frequency — all of which are reported as satisfactory in this scenario. Fetal heart rate is recorded elsewhere.
Incorrect. The maternal condition section monitors the mother's vitals (pulse, blood pressure, temperature, urine output). A fetal heart rate abnormality would not be detected in this section.
Incorrect. The cervicograph is a component WITHIN the progress of labour section — it plots cervical dilatation against time. It does not record fetal heart rate.

overallFeedback.feedback: The WHO partograph has three sections: (1) fetal condition — FHR, liquor colour, moulding; (2) progress of labour — cervicograph, descent, contractions; and (3) maternal condition — vitals, urine. A fetal heart rate drop is detected in the fetal condition section, regardless of what the cervicograph shows.

Well done. The WHO partograph separates monitoring into three distinct sections — fetal condition, progress of labour, and maternal condition — precisely so that abnormalities in one dimension are identified even when the others appear reassuring.

interactions.label: On vaginal examination of a woman in early labour, you find a diagonal conjugate

params.question: On vaginal examination of a woman in early labour, you find a diagonal conjugate of 11 cm. What is the most appropriate clinical interpretation of this finding?

answers.text: The obstetric conjugate is approximately 11 cm, which is adequate for vaginal delivery

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. The obstetric conjugate is NOT the same as the diagonal conjugate — it is estimated by subtracting 1.5–2 cm from the diagonal conjugate. A diagonal conjugate of 11 cm gives an obstetric conjugate of approximately 9–9.5 cm, not 11 cm.

answers.text: The obstetric conjugate is approximately 9–9.5 cm, indicating a contracted inlet that requires close monitoring

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The obstetric conjugate (true anteroposterior diameter of the inlet) is estimated by subtracting 1.5–2 cm from the diagonal conjugate. At 9–9.5 cm (normal ≥10 cm), the inlet is contracted — the head may not engage without significant moulding, warranting close monitoring and early senior involvement.

answers.text: The diagonal conjugate cannot reliably be used to estimate the obstetric conjugate

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. The diagonal conjugate is the only directly measurable anteroposterior diameter of the inlet on vaginal examination. The obstetric conjugate is routinely estimated from it by subtracting 1.5–2 cm — this is a fundamental clinical skill.

answers.text: A diagonal conjugate of 11 cm confirms a gynecoid pelvis favourable for vaginal delivery

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. The diagonal conjugate measures one diameter of the inlet, not pelvic type. A gynecoid pelvis is characterised by its shape — round or oval inlet, straight sidewalls, non-prominent ischial spines, and a wide sub-pubic arch — not by a single measurement.

overallFeedback.feedback: The obstetric conjugate is estimated by subtracting 1.5–2 cm from the diagonal conjugate. With a diagonal conjugate of 11 cm, the obstetric conjugate is approximately 9–9.5 cm (normal ≥10 cm), indicating a contracted pelvic inlet. The student must recognise this reasoning chain to anticipate difficulty with engagement and plan accordingly.

Excellent clinical reasoning. Subtracting 1.5–2 cm from a diagonal conjugate of 11 cm gives an obstetric conjugate of 9–9.5 cm — below the normal minimum of 10 cm. This contracted inlet demands careful monitoring of descent and early senior consultation.
